---
title: "A tour of the estimators"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 96)
set.seed(2026)
```

tsorder answers one question — *how many terms does this series need?* —
with three families of estimators that answer it in different senses. This
article walks through all of them on simulated data where the truth is
known. The design principle shared by everything in the package: **every
threshold lives on a studentised scale** (each statistic is divided by its
own null standard error), so "above the threshold" means the same thing for
every statistic, every process and every scale.

```{r}
library(tsorder)
```

## Information criteria: penalised fit

The classical answer. Fit AR(0..K), charge each order a penalty, keep the
argmin. All seven criteria (AIC, AICc, BIC, HQ, FPE, CAT, MDL) share one
Levinson recursion, so asking for all of them costs one pass.

```{r criteria}
x <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = c(1.2, -0.6)), 800))
fit <- order_select(x, "bic")
fit
autoplot(fit)
```

## Threshold ("clip") estimators: the last lag noise cannot explain

The Fine–Hwang (1979) family: let the inspected memory `p_n` grow with the
sample (default `⌈2 log n⌉`), studentise a statistic lag by lag, zero out
everything below a slowly-growing threshold, and report the last survivor.
The default statistic is the PACF, which is *self-studentised*: beyond the
true order its fluctuation is `1/√n` whatever the process (Quenouille).

```{r fh}
fit <- order_select(x, "pacf")
fit
autoplot(fit)
```

Each statistic targets a family: `pacf`, `jirak` and `long_ar_ols` read AR
orders; `acf_bartlett` and `inverse_pacf` read MA orders.

```{r ma}
y <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ma = c(0.9, 0.5)), 800))
c(ma_by_acf  = order_select(y, "acf_bartlett")$order,
  ma_by_ipacf = order_select(y, "inverse_pacf")$order,
  ar_bic_overshoots = ic_order(y, "bic")$order)  # an MA is an AR(Inf)
```

The last line is the point of having both families: an MA(2) *is* an
AR(∞), so an AR criterion dutifully reports a long autoregression, while
the MA-targeted statistics read 2.

### Jirak's refitted estimator

`jirak_order()` refits the Yule–Walker autoregression at every dimension
`k ≤ p_n`, studentises each coefficient vector exactly, and takes the
largest per-dimension estimate — extra power when a coefficient is small in
the long-AR representation, at O(p_n⁴) cost (negligible at the poly-log
default).

```{r jirak}
jirak_order(x)$order
order_select(x, "jirak_refit")
```

### Robust statistics for contaminated series

Five percent of additive outliers is enough to erase the classical PACF.
The robust statistics (`pacf_robust`, `acf_robust`) replace the sample
autocorrelation with the Ma–Genton Q_n-ratio form, whose shared
denominator cancels the outlier bias. They are marked experimental: their
studentisations are Monte Carlo-calibrated, pending exact theory.

```{r robust}
clean <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = c(1.2, -0.6)), 2000))
spikes <- rbinom(2000, 1, 0.05) * rnorm(2000, sd = 10)
dirty <- clean + spikes

c(classical_clean = order_select(clean, "pacf")$order,
  classical_dirty = order_select(dirty, "pacf")$order,
  robust_dirty    = order_select(dirty, "pacf_robust")$order)
```

## McMillan degree: an order that survives measurement noise

Adding observation noise to an AR(2) makes the observed series an
ARMA(2, 2) — every AR-order selector then has a different *true* answer.
The McMillan degree (the state dimension, `max(p, q)` for an ARMA) does not
move. `svc` is Bauer's (2001) canonical-correlation estimator of it.

```{r mcmillan}
ar2 <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = c(1.2, -0.6)), 3000))
noisy <- ar2 + rnorm(3000, sd = 0.5 * sd(ar2))

c(svc_clean = order_select(ar2, "svc")$order,
  svc_noisy = order_select(noisy, "svc")$order,   # still the degree
  pacf_noisy = order_select(noisy, "pacf")$order) # answers a different question
```

## ARMA (p, q) jointly

Two identifiers: the EACF table of Tsay and Tiao (vertex read
automatically), and Hannan–Rissanen (with the published 1983 correction
pass, on by default — see the benchmark article for why it matters).

```{r arma}
z <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.4), 1500))
eacf(z)$order
hannan_rissanen(z)[c("p", "q")]
```

## From selection to a fitted model

`integration_order()` estimates `d` by sequential KPSS testing with a
vanishing level; `fit_arima()` chains everything and returns a plain
`stats::arima` fit, so `predict()`, `forecast::forecast()` and broom all
apply.

```{r fit}
w <- cumsum(z)  # integrate once
integration_order(w)$d
fit <- fit_arima(w, method = "hr")
fit
```

In a tidyverts pipeline, the same chain is available as a `fabletools`
model:

```{r fable, eval = requireNamespace("fabletools", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("tsibble", quietly = TRUE)}
df <- tsibble::tsibble(idx = seq_along(w), value = w, index = idx)
fabletools::model(df, tsorder = TSORDER(value))
```

## Choosing among them

* Stationary, clean, AR-like: the default `order_select(x)` (PACF clip) or
  `ic_order(x, "bic")` — they agree far more often than not.
* MA order: `acf_bartlett` or `inverse_pacf`.
* `p` and `q` together: `hannan_rissanen`, or `eacf` to *see* the table.
* Outliers or heavy tails: `pacf_robust` / `acf_robust`.
* Measurement noise, or you need the state dimension: `svc`.
* Unsure about stationarity: `integration_order()` first, or let
  `fit_arima()` handle the whole chain.

The defaults behind each of these choices were fixed by the simulation
benchmark described in [the benchmark article](benchmark.html).
